Recommended varieties
Gijnlim

An early, all-male hybrid producing green spears. A strong first choice for a productive, permanent asparagus bed.

Connover's Colossal

A long-established asparagus with substantial green spears. Keep as the traditional alternative to modern all-male hybrids.

Key risks
VIOLET ROOT ROT

Purple fungal growth on roots, with yellowing and dying fern, can indicate violet root rot.

FROST

Young shoots may turn black and die if a severe frost occurs in late spring.

PERENNIAL WEEDS

Couch grass, bindweed and other perennial weeds are a serious long-term problem in asparagus beds.

SLUGS

Spears are gnawed, making them unfit for table use.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
14
STALKS & SHOOTS

Good drainage is essential.

Choose a sunny, sheltered site and enrich the soil with compost or well-rotted manure.

Clear perennial weeds before planting.

A light-excluding mulch for a whole season is worthwhile on badly infested ground.

Plant crowns in early spring.

Delay if the soil is cold and wet; keep bought crowns moist.

Soil & preparation
Choose sunny, sheltered, well-drained soil. Add compost or rotted manure; lime very acid ground if needed. Improve heavy-ground drainage or use a raised bed.
Clear perennial weeds first: their roots are hard to remove once tangled with crowns.
Sowing & planting
1 Prepare a mound

Keep crowns moist. Mound fine soil in the clean, well-drained trench.

2 Spread the roots

Spread roots over the mound, with the crown above the root ends.

3 Cover the roots

Cover roots; leave bud tips visible. Water to settle; keep mulch off growth points.

Trench Dig 12 in. wide and 8 in. deep; centres 18 in. apart. Stagger plants in adjacent trenches.
Initial cover Cover roots; leave bud tips visible

From seed: sow thinly in spring, thin and grow on. Plant into the final bed next spring; cropping starts later than with crowns.

Looking after the crop
Hand-weed or hoe shallowly to protect roots. Water in dry spells, especially while plants establish. Mulch mature beds against weeds, keeping growth points clear. Strong summer ferns build next spring’s reserves.
Each year, mulch established beds with 1–2 in. of compost or well-rotted manure. Tidy and lightly feed with compost before spears appear.
Support tall ferns if needed. Remove berries before they fall and seed into the bed. Let ferns yellow before cutting down; remove diseased growth.
Harvesting & storage
Wait two years after planting crowns, or three years from seed. Let uncut spears form fern to build strong roots.
Cut finger-thick spears by 7 in. tall, about 1 in. below soil, before they turn woody. Use a sharp knife, avoiding nearby shoots. Check every few days in cool weather, daily in warmth.
Cut for six weeks in the first harvest year, then up to eight weeks. Stop by mid-June, sooner if weak, and let later spears form fern.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
VIOLET ROOT ROT	Roots develop purple mould; foliage yellows and dies.	Confirm diagnosis; remove affected crowns and replant on clean ground.
FROST	Young shoots turn black and die after late spring frost.	Remove damaged shoots and cover the bed if hard frost is forecast.
PERENNIAL WEEDS	Couch, bindweed and other perennial weeds invade the crowns.	Clear them before planting; later removal risks crop damage.
SLUGS	Spears are gnawed and become unfit to eat.	Check shoots on damp evenings, hand-pick slugs and encourage natural predators.
Final tips

Treat the bed as a permanent feature: clean ground and patience pay off.

Strong summer fern growth feeds the crowns for next spring.

Key risks
Black Bean Aphid

Black aphids cluster on soft tips, especially on spring-sown broad beans.

Chocolate Spot

Small chocolate-brown spots appear on leaves, with dark streaks along the stems; pods and seeds may also be marked.

No Pods

Flowers fall without forming pods.

Pea and Bean Weevil

U-shaped notches mark young leaves; seedlings may be badly damaged.

18
PEAS & BEANS

Rich soil, without waterlogging.

Moisture-retentive, free-draining ground suits broad beans.

Support tall varieties.

Stakes and strings keep plants upright in wind.

Pinch out the soft tops.

Do this at full flower or when the first pods form to discourage blackfly.

Soil & preparation
Sun; moist, drained soil without last year’s beans. Lime very acid soil to pH 6.5.
Use ground enriched for an earlier crop. Add autumn compost or rotted manure to poor soil.
Sowing & planting
1 Sow large beans

Sow in prepared soil; add spare seeds at row ends for filling gaps.

2 Establish a double row

Pair rows; wider gaps between pairs. Stake tall plants.

Within each row pair 9 in. between the two rows of a pair

Cold, heavy soil or mice: start in pots/modules under glass; plant when conditions improve.

Sow hardy varieties in late autumn only in mild districts. Wait for spring on cold or wet ground.

Looking after the crop
Weed; earth up lightly. Dwarfs need little support. In wind, string tall plants between stout end stakes; add stakes along long rows.
Water deeply in dry spells from flowering to pod swelling; mulch. Check seedlings and pots for earlier watering.
Pinch soft tops at full flower/first pods to discourage black bean aphid. Cook tops like spinach.
After cropping, cut stems at soil level. Leave roots and nodules; chop stems for compost.
Harvesting & storage
Pick regularly before pods become large and leathery. Very small pods with pea-sized beans can be cooked whole.
Shelling: pick when beans show through pods, before scars darken. Twist down sharply; older beans lose sweetness and become starchier.
For dried winter beans, mature pods on plants if weather permits; finish drying in airy shelter, then shell and store.

Chocolate Spot	Brown spots on leaves and stems.	Remove severe attacks; improve spacing and rotate.
No Pods	Flowers fall without pods.	Mulch and water roots well from flowering.
Pea and Bean Weevil	Notches in young leaf edges.	Water seedlings in drought; protect with fine mesh.
Birds	Torn pods	Protect seed and seedlings with netting or guards.
Mice	Seeds or seedlings vanish overnight.	Trap mice; raise seed in modules; protect sowings.
Bean Seed Fly	Tunnelled seeds and seedlings.	Remove damaged seedlings; plant module-raised beans.
Foot Rot and Root Rot	Dark, rotting roots and stem bases.	Remove affected plants; improve drainage; rotate.

Sow spare seeds to fill gaps.

Wide rows of tall beans can shelter lower follow-on crops.

PEAS & BEANS

Wait for warmth.

Cold, wet ground can rot seed; plant out after frost danger has passed.

Protect young seedlings.

Keep beds clean and weed-free, and watch for slugs.

Water from flowering.

Dry roots can cause flower drop and poor pod set.

Soil & preparation
Warm, sheltered sun; light, well-drained soil. Add compost or rotted manure; avoid cold, wet clay. Lime only if too acid.
Avoid last year’s bean bed. Climbers need richer, moister soil than dwarfs: enrich a trench or strip on poor ground.
Sowing & planting
1 Sow in warm soil

After frosts, sow 2 beans per station in warm soil. For early crops, raise under glass; harden off to plant.

2 Keep the strongest

Keep the stronger seedling. Grow dwarfs in rows or blocks; support climbers early.

Dwarf blocks: plants 6 in. each way
Climbing supports 6 in. between canes; retain one plant per cane

Sow outdoors from late May; repeat late June/early July. Quick facts spacing is for dwarfs in rows.

For early crops, warm soil under cloches in March, sow in April; uncover in late May.

Looking after the crop
Protect seedlings from slugs; keep beds clean and weed-free, especially below low dwarf pods.
Dwarf varieties normally need no support. Give climbers canes, netting, wigwams or strings early; guide wandering shoots onto them.
Water regularly from flowering in dry weather. Warmth and steady root moisture improve pod set more than spraying flowers; dry roots cause flower drop, especially on vigorous climbers.
Water and use an organic liquid feed after the first flush of pods to encourage a smaller second crop.
Harvesting & storage
Pick tender green pods every few days before the beans inside swell. Search carefully for pods hidden in climbing foliage.
Dwarfs usually crop first, for about four to six weeks; replace tired plants with a later sowing. Climbers may crop for six to ten weeks with regular picking and watering.
For dried haricots, let pods ripen straw-coloured. If needed, hang plants upside down in an airy shed to finish drying. Shell; dry beans fully before airtight storage.
Pests & diseases

Black Bean Aphid	Black colonies on soft growth.	Squash damaging colonies; allow predators.
No Pods	Flowers fall without pods.	Mulch and water roots well from flowering.
Pea and Bean Weevil	Notches in young leaf edges.	Water seedlings in drought; protect with fine mesh.
Birds	Torn pods	Protect seed and seedlings with netting, guards, twigs or black cotton.
Mice	Missing seed or seedlings before establishment.	Trap mice; raise seed in modules; protect sowings.
Halo Blight	Leaf spots with yellow halos.	Remove diseased plants; use clean seed; rotate.
Bean Seed Fly	Tunnelled seeds and seedlings.	Remove damaged seedlings; plant module-raised beans.
Final tips

Pick before beans swell inside pods.

Give climbers supports at sowing or planting time.
